learn.intro: After Stalin's death, a 'thaw' and Khrushchev's peaceful co-existence alternated with dangerous crises over Hungary, Berlin and Cuba. By 1964 the hot-line and Test Ban Treaty showed lessons had been learned — but China was now a nuclear power and a rival to Moscow.

sections.title: 1. Personalities, summits and peaceful co-existence

blocks.p: Eisenhower (US President 1953–61) and his Secretary of State John Foster Dulles (to 1959) combined a hard line — 'massive retaliation' (1954) and brinkmanship — with willingness to talk. Khrushchev emerged as Soviet leader after 1953 and at the 20th Party Congress (February 1956) denounced Stalin and promoted 'peaceful co-existence': competition with the West without war.

Summits: Geneva (July 1955) produced little agreement but a friendlier 'spirit of Geneva'. Khrushchev visited the USA in September 1959 (Camp David). The Paris Summit (May 1960) collapsed after an American U-2 spy plane was shot down over the USSR on 1 May 1960. Kennedy's first meeting with Khrushchev at Vienna (June 1961) went badly and preceded the Berlin Wall.

Kennedy (1961–63) promised 'flexible response' instead of all-or-nothing nuclear threats, but also suffered the failed Bay of Pigs invasion (April 1961). Macmillan, British Prime Minister 1957–63, visited Moscow in 1959 and pressed for a test ban. Mao increasingly rejected peaceful co-existence as betrayal of revolution.

evidence: 1 May 1960: U-2 shot down; Paris Summit collapses.

sections.title: 2. Developments along the Iron Curtain

blocks.p: Austria: the Austrian State Treaty (May 1955) ended four-power occupation; Soviet troops withdrew and Austria became neutral. Reasons: to show peaceful co-existence in action, to encourage a neutral Germany, and because Austria was of limited strategic value. Impact: an early sign of the thaw, but also the creation of the Warsaw Pact (May 1955) the same month.

Hungary 1956: inspired by de-Stalinisation, Hungarians rose in October 1956. Imre Nagy announced Hungary would leave the Warsaw Pact; Soviet tanks crushed the rising from 4 November, with thousands killed. The West, distracted by Suez and unwilling to risk war, did not intervene — showing that the USA accepted the Soviet sphere in practice despite talk of 'rolling back' communism.

Berlin 1958–61: millions of East Germans fled to the West through Berlin, a 'brain drain'. In November 1958 Khrushchev issued an ultimatum demanding Western troops leave within six months; it lapsed. On 13 August 1961 East Germany sealed the border and built the Berlin Wall. Tank stand-off at Checkpoint Charlie (October 1961). The Wall stopped the exodus and, ironically, stabilised the crisis; Kennedy visited West Berlin in June 1963.

evidence: May 1955: Austrian State Treaty; Warsaw Pact.

blocks.p: Weapons and delivery: the USA tested a hydrogen bomb in 1952 and the USSR in 1953. The Soviet Sputnik satellite (October 1957) showed it could build long-range rockets, causing American fears of a 'missile gap' (in fact the USA had more missiles). Intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs), long-range bombers and, from 1960, US Polaris submarine missiles made nuclear war faster and harder to defend against.

The Cuban Missile Crisis (October 1962): after the Bay of Pigs, the USSR secretly placed nuclear missiles on Cuba. US U-2 photographs revealed them on 14 October; Kennedy imposed a naval 'quarantine'. After thirteen days, Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles in return for a US pledge not to invade Cuba, with a secret promise to remove US Jupiter missiles from Turkey.

Significance: both sides recognised how close they had come. The Washington–Moscow 'hot-line' was agreed in June 1963 for direct communication; the Partial Test Ban Treaty (August 1963) banned tests in the atmosphere, in space and under water. But China refused to sign and exploded its first atomic bomb in October 1964.

sections.title: 4. The beginnings of the Sino-Soviet split

blocks.p: Reasons: Mao resented Khrushchev's attack on Stalin and his peaceful co-existence; disputes over Soviet nuclear help (withdrawn in 1959); Soviet criticism of the Great Leap Forward; rivalry for leadership of world communism; Khrushchev's climb-down in Cuba, which Mao mocked. In 1960 the USSR withdrew its advisers from China.

Impact on East–West relations: the communist world was no longer a single bloc. Moscow had new reasons to stabilise relations with the West, while China's hostility to both superpowers and its bomb (1964) made the Cold War a three-cornered contest — preparing the ground for later US approaches to China.

vocab.def: Khrushchev's policy of competition with the West without war.
Pushing a crisis to the edge of war to force the other side to back down.

misconceptions.wrong: Peaceful co-existence meant the end of rivalry.
misconceptions.right: It meant competition without war — crises over Berlin and Cuba still happened.

misconceptions.wrong: The USA tried to help Hungary in 1956.
misconceptions.right: It did not intervene, showing acceptance of the Soviet sphere.

flashcards.a: Khrushchev's policy (from 1956) of competition with the West without war.

flashcards.q: Why did the USSR withdraw from Austria?
flashcards.a: To show peaceful co-existence, encourage a neutral Germany, limited strategic value.
Showed the USSR would use force to keep its satellites; the West would not intervene.

flashcards.q: Significance of the Cuban Missile Crisis?
flashcards.a: Closest to nuclear war; led to the hot-line and Partial Test Ban Treaty; damaged Khrushchev.

flashcards.q: How did the Sino-Soviet split affect East–West relations?
flashcards.a: Ended a single communist bloc; three-cornered Cold War; Moscow had reasons to stabilise relations with the West.

checklist.text: I can explain the role of Eisenhower, Dulles, Kennedy, Khrushchev, Mao and Macmillan, and the impact of summits.
I can explain developments in Austria, Hungary and Berlin 1955–61.
I can judge the significance of the Cuban Missile Crisis and the agreements that followed.
I can explain the reasons for the Sino-Soviet split and its impact on East–West relations.
